body.heading: Blending with the background
paragraphs: Camouflage is the art of not being noticed. The simplest method is matching: a green caterpillar on a green leaf, a sandy-coloured lizard on desert ground, a snow-white Arctic hare in winter. Predators hunt largely by sight, so an animal that merges with its background may simply never be seen.

Many animals are countershaded — dark on top, pale underneath, like sharks, penguins and deer. Seen from above they match the dark depths or ground; from below, the pale belly matches bright surface light. The shading also cancels the shadows that would reveal a solid body.

body.heading: Breaking the outline
paragraphs: Matching colour is not the only trick. Bold stripes and blotches can work by disruption: they break up the animal's outline so the eye cannot assemble it into a recognisable shape. A zebra's stripes may serve this purpose in a herd, where outlines dissolve into a shifting pattern.

Some animals go further and change. Chameleons shift colour by adjusting pigment cells in their skin, and cuttlefish — though colour-blind themselves — can repaint their skin with moving patterns in a second, copying the seabed they hover over.

body.heading: An arms race of eyes and disguises
paragraphs: Camouflage serves hunters as well as the hunted: a tiger's stripes vanish into tall grass light, letting it approach unseen. And disguises keep evolving against sharper eyes — some moths match not just colour but the texture of bark, complete with fake lichen patches.

Seasonal costume changes show the stakes. The snowshoe hare turns white for winter and brown for summer; if snow comes late, a white hare on dark ground is dangerously visible — camouflage only works when it matches the calendar too.

takeaway: Camouflage hides animals by matching background colours and patterns or breaking up their outline; some animals can even change their appearance to suit a new background.
